implementation_notes: In Ruby the object-mother role is played by fixtures tooling rather than a hand-written class: factory_bot defines declarative factories (FactoryBot.define { factory :customer { name { "Ada" } } }) with build/create/stub strategies, inheritance and traits for variation, and is the community's replacement for hand-rolled XxxMother classes. Prefer traits and transient attributes over adding more named factories as variation grows; a hand-written mother remains justifiable only in a plain minitest project that refuses external gems.
pitfalls: create persists through the database and runs callbacks; cascading associations make tests slow and order-dependent unless transactional tests are enabled.
build vs create: a built object has no id and no associated rows, so code paths that expect persisted state fail in confusing ways.
Sequences keep counting for the whole process, so assertions on generated emails or ids must not assume start values.
Factories defined with strings for associations or callbacks couples fixture definitions to model internals and breaks when those change.

variants.name: Rails YAML fixture files
variants.idiom_name: test/fixtures/*.yml rows loaded into the test database
variants.implementation_notes: Rails' built-in fixtures are the zero-dependency form: named rows in test/fixtures/*.yml are inserted into the test database before each test class runs, giving every test the same ready-made records by fixture name (customers(:ada)). Use them for small, stable canonical data sets and switch to factory_bot as soon as you need per-test variation, computed attributes or objects that must not touch the database.
variants.code_sketch:
# test/fixtures/customers.yml
ada:
  id: 7
  name: Ada Lovelace
  tier: vip

# test/models/invoice_test.rb
class InvoiceTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  test "vip gets a discount" do
    assert Invoice.for_customer(customers(:ada)).has_discount?
  end
end
pitfalls: Fixture rows bypass validations and callbacks, so they can represent states the application would reject; keep them realistic.
All fixtures for a test class are loaded before every test, which slows large suites and couples tests to rows they never use unless fixtures :all is narrowed.
Fixture data is global and static: two tests needing the same model in different states must either add rows or edit the shared ones.
